newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - De Swaan heads bank regulators group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - De Swaan heads bank regulators group.

text.p: Tom de Swaan of the Dutch central bank will become the new chairman of a group of national bank regulators who have developed global supervisory guidelines, together with emerging countries, to prevent financial crises.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Monday said central bank governors from the G10 group of industrial nations had appointed De Swaan, 51 to succeed the Bank of Italy's highly-respected Tommaso Padoa-Schioppa.

De Swaan becomes chairman of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, a forum for cooperation among national bank regulators that was formed by G10 in 1974. It has no formal supranational authority but formulates standards followed not only by G10 countries but most countries worldwide.

Tietmeyer also said the G10 central bank governors had endorsed a set of core principles for worldwide banking supervision that will now be presented to an annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Hong Kong.

The principles are part of the IMF's new strategy to prevent future financial crises and represent the first substantial move to set global guidelines for banking supervisors from industrial nations as well as the emerging economies in Asia and Latin America and transition economies in Eastern Europe.

International policy makers from the IMF and Group of Seven (G7) have launched an aggressive effort to strengthen bank supervision in emerging countries to prevent new international crises following Mexico's financial problems in late 1994.

De Swaan, director of banking supervision at the Dutch central bank, is currently chairman of the Joint Forum of Supervisors, a group charged with increasing cooperation between supervisors of the bank, securities and insurance sectors.

A report on this growing cross-sector cooperation and efforts by the Basle Committee to improve world banking supervision was also discussed by G10 central bank governors and will be presented to the G7 summit in June in Denver, Colorado.

Details of the banking principles will be released on Wednesday. Tietmeyer said he hoped the consultative process with the banking industry would be completed before the IMF's September meeting so the principles could be finalised.

"This paper has not only been drafted by the Basle Committee, but also with non-G10 supervisors and we hope this will be the paper that represents core principles agreed by supervisors all over the world," Tietmeyer said.

Tietmeyer was speaking in his capacity as chairman of the G10 central bank governors' committee after its monthly meeting at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the worlds' central banks.
De Swaan was picked after Padoa-Schioppa, who has headed the Basle Committee since 1993, was named by the Italian goverrment to head Consob, Italy's stock market regulator.
The Basle Committee is best known for the 1988 Capital Accord, which required international banks to set aside a capital cushion of a minimum eight percent of risk-weighted assets.
But while the Capital Accord halted the decline in bank capital levels, which by the late 1980s was threatening the safety of financial systems, it is no longer seen as adequate.

De Swaan is likely to start working on devising new regulatory standards that are more useful in determining the soundness of today's sophisticated banking groups, which some central bankers feel have outpaced regulators in accurately measuring credit risks, still the main source of losses for banks.
In addition to being chairman of the Joint Forum, he was already a member of the Basle Committee and chairman of the European Monetary Institute's banking supervisory sub-committee.
The G10 comprises 11 countries, the G7 -- the U.S., Japan, Canada, Germany, Britain, France and Italy -- as well the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.
